1.text: It’s the weekend. You see a limited-edition item you really like, but it costs 30% more than your monthly budget. What would you do?

options.A: Buy it immediately — if I miss it now, it’s gone.
options.B: Walk away and review next month’s budget to see if I can afford it.
options.C: Decide I don’t really need it after all.
options.D: Check its resale value; if it holds value well, I’ll buy it.

2.text: You have some spare cash and can choose only one of the following:

options.A: Invest in a friend’s project — it could increase fivefold in one year or lose everything.
options.B: Put it into a stable investment with a guaranteed 4.5% annual return.

3.text: While scrolling on your phone, you see content titled “How to Achieve Financial Freedom by Age 30.” What is your most likely reaction?

options.A: Carefully study the financial concepts mentioned (e.g., volatility, Sharpe ratio).
options.B: Save it for later, though I haven’t put it into practice.
options.C: Assume it’s anxiety-driven marketing and scroll past.
options.D: Take out paper or a calculator to estimate my own financial gap.

4.text: A highly accurate fortune-teller lets you see one moment of your future. What do you most want to see?

options.A: Myself at age 60, financially secure with a well-planned retirement.
options.B: Myself one year from now, freely spending this money on travel or leisure.
options.C: Confirmation that next month’s bills are fully paid.

5.text: You order an extremely expensive but bad-tasting dish at a restaurant (non-refundable). What do you do?

options.A: Finish it — every bite represents money.
options.B: Stop eating; the money is already gone, and my health matters more.
options.C: Try to fix it with extra seasoning, even if it likely won’t help.

6.text: Compared to having a large sum of money ten years from now, I care more about being able to enjoy life and travel freely right now.

7.text: I enjoy the excitement of searching for opportunities in uncertain or volatile markets.

8.text: If I overspend unexpectedly, I feel noticeable guilt for several days afterward.

9.text: Which of the following describe your current behavior? (Select all that apply.)

options.A: I subscribe to at least two in-depth finance newsletters or research reports.
options.B: I regularly use tools (e.g., Excel, apps) to track my net worth.
options.C: I understand asset allocation and hold at least three different asset types.
options.D: I frequently rebalance my portfolio based on market trends.

10.text: During large promotions (e.g., Black Friday), which behaviors apply to you? (Select all that apply.)

options.A: I plan purchases in advance and stick strictly to my list.
options.B: I feel overwhelmed by discount rules and buy casually.
options.C: I stay up late watching livestreams and buy due to the atmosphere.
options.D: I calculate post-discount prices and avoid buying if the cost of holding inventory is too high.

11.text: If I suddenly receive unexpected money, my first thought is how to spend it rather than how to save it.

12.text: I believe insurance is mostly unnecessary or a waste of money for low-probability events.

13.text: I rarely check shopping app notifications; my purchases are usually initiated by active searching.

14.text: Saving money now feels meaningless because inflation will erode future purchasing power anyway.

15.text: If a long-term asset I hold drops 20% in a single month, I become so anxious that it affects my sleep.

AFDE.name: The Sovereign
AFDE.description: Top strategist who uses extreme discipline to navigate risk and build a financial empire.

AFDN.name: The Visionary
AFDN.description: Ambitious yet inexperienced, you rely on intuition and remarkable perseverance for long-term investments, trading time for returns.

AFIE.name: The Hunter
AFIE.description: Knowledgeable but occasionally impulsive, you'll go all-in for future game-changing opportunities.

AFIN.name: The Dreamer
AFIN.description: Dreams of future wealth but has a short memory. Can't control spending impulses and repeatedly falls for high-risk financial schemes.

APDE.name: The Striker
APDE.description: Extremely disciplined short-term expert who precisely captures profits in market volatility.

APDN.name: The Adventurer
APDN.description: Enjoys fresh money-making opportunities. Not very professional but disciplined enough to avoid major losses.

APIE.name: The High Roller
APIE.description: Understands money and loves the thrill it brings. Spends lavishly while earning through high-risk ventures.

APIN.name: The Firework
APIN.description: Classic hedonist who neither understands nor controls money. Lives for the moment.

GFDE.name: The Fortress
GFDE.description: Highly professional and disciplined long-term investor. A compounding machine.

GFDN.name: The Dam-Builder
GFDN.description: Doesn't understand complex finance but accumulates wealth through saving and thrift instincts.

GFIE.name: The Sentinel
GFIE.description: Understands finance but has weak psychological resilience. Thinks long-term but often anxious about market swings.

GFIN.name: The Ostrich
GFIN.description: Extremely risk-averse with poor self-control. Refuses to engage with finances and only trusts bank deposits.

GPDE.name: The Optimizer
GPDE.description: Extremely shrewd, scrutinizing every expense with professional insight. Lives with extreme rigor.

GPDN.name: The Minimalist
GPDN.description: Doesn't want to study money. Lives a simple, stable life through low desires and self-discipline.

GPIE.name: The Savvy Shopper
GPIE.description: Knows all financial tricks but prioritizes current desires over professional knowledge.

GPIN.name: The Drifter
GPIN.description: Follows the crowd with finances. Fears loss but wants to buy. Financial state depends entirely on today's mood.

glossary.Gross Pay: Your earnings before taxes and deductions are taken out.
glossary.Net Pay: The amount that actually lands in your bank account after deductions.
glossary.Taxable Income: The portion of your income subject to income tax after eligible adjustments or pre-tax deductions.
glossary.Withholding: Money taken from your paycheck in advance to cover taxes.
glossary.W-4: A form used to help determine federal tax withholding from your paycheck.
glossary.FICA: Payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare.
glossary.Pre-tax Deduction: A deduction taken before some taxes are calculated.
glossary.Pay Stub: A record showing gross pay, deductions, taxes, and net pay.
glossary.Fixed Expense: A cost that stays about the same each month, such as rent.
glossary.Variable Expense: A cost that changes month to month, such as groceries or gas.
glossary.Security Deposit: Money paid upfront to protect a landlord against damage or unpaid rent.
glossary.Checking Account: A bank account used for everyday spending and bill payments.
glossary.Savings Account: A bank account designed to hold money and usually earn interest.
glossary.Debit Card: A card linked to your checking account; purchases come directly from your balance.
glossary.Credit Card: A borrowing tool with a limit; unpaid balances may accrue interest.
glossary.APR: Annual Percentage Rate, the yearly cost of borrowing on a credit card or loan.
glossary.Credit Utilization: The percentage of your available credit currently being used.
glossary.Statement Balance: The amount owed on your card at the end of a billing cycle.
glossary.Minimum Payment: The smallest payment required to keep a credit card account current.
glossary.Annual Fee: A yearly fee charged by some credit cards.
glossary.Foreign Transaction Fee: A fee charged by some cards for purchases in another country or currency.
glossary.Premium: The amount you pay regularly to keep insurance coverage active.
glossary.Deductible: The amount you pay before insurance starts sharing covered costs.
glossary.Copay: A fixed amount you pay for a covered medical service.
glossary.Coinsurance: The percentage of covered medical costs you pay after meeting your deductible.
glossary.Out-of-Pocket Maximum: The most you pay in a plan year for covered healthcare before the insurer pays 100% of covered costs.
glossary.In-Network: Doctors and providers that have negotiated prices with your insurance plan.
glossary.401(k): An employer-sponsored retirement account that may include employer matching.
glossary.Employer Match: Money your employer contributes to your retirement account based on your contribution.
glossary.Renter Insurance: Insurance that helps cover your belongings and personal liability while renting.
glossary.Auto Insurance: Insurance that may cover vehicle damage, liability, and related losses.
glossary.Emergency Fund: Savings reserved for urgent, unexpected expenses.
glossary.Liquidity: How quickly you can access money without losing value.
glossary.Phishing: A scam that tricks you into revealing information through fake emails, texts, or websites.
glossary.Identity Theft: When someone uses your personal information without permission.
glossary.Credit Freeze: A restriction on access to your credit report to help prevent fraudulent new accounts.
glossary.Experian: One of the three major U.S. credit bureaus.
glossary.Equifax: One of the three major U.S. credit bureaus.
glossary.TransUnion: One of the three major U.S. credit bureaus.
glossary.HSA: A Health Savings Account used with qualifying health plans for eligible medical expenses.
glossary.Certificate of Deposit: A bank product with a fixed term and usually a fixed interest rate.
glossary.RSU: Restricted Stock Unit, a company stock grant that usually vests over time.
glossary.Fund: An investment vehicle, such as an ETF or mutual fund, that holds many underlying investments.
glossary.Diversification: Spreading investments across assets to reduce concentration risk.
glossary.APY: Annual Percentage Yield, the yearly return on a deposit including compounding.
glossary.Direct Deposit: Electronic deposit of pay into your bank account.
glossary.Overdraft: When a transaction exceeds the available balance in your checking account.
glossary.Due Date: The date by which a bill or payment must be made.
glossary.RSU Vesting: The schedule that determines when you actually gain ownership of granted company shares.

modules.title: 1. Paycheck & Taxes
modules.shortDescription: Understand how compensation becomes take-home pay.

lessonBlocks.heading: Gross pay, net pay, and why your first deposit looks smaller
paragraphs: As a new grad, one of the first surprises is that your salary offer is not what lands in your bank account. Your paycheck starts with [[Gross Pay]], then subtracts taxes, benefits, and other deductions before you receive [[Net Pay]].
Your monthly budget should be built from net pay, not from annual salary or gross pay. That keeps rent, bills, and savings plans grounded in the money you actually have.
bullets: Gross pay is before deductions
Net pay is what you can actually spend or save
Always budget using net pay

questions.title: Question 1
questions.prompt: Which number should you use to build your monthly budget?
questions.explanation: Your budget should be based on the money you actually receive: net pay.

choices.text: The amount before taxes plus estimated bonus

questions.title: Question 2
questions.prompt: Which statement is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Net pay is gross pay minus taxes and deductions.

choices.text: Gross pay is always lower than net pay
Salary offer equals monthly spendable cash
Net pay is what remains after taxes and deductions

lessonBlocks.heading: Taxable income, withholding, and FICA
paragraphs: Many early-career workers treat taxes as one single line, but your paycheck often includes different categories. [[Withholding]] is money taken out in advance for income taxes. [[FICA]] covers Social Security and Medicare.
[[Taxable Income]] is the portion of income actually subject to income tax. Some [[Pre-tax Deduction]] items can reduce taxable income before tax is calculated.
bullets: FICA is separate from income tax withholding
Taxable income can be lower than gross income
Pre-tax deductions may reduce some tax exposure

questions.title: Question 3
questions.prompt: What is withholding?
questions.explanation: Withholding is money taken from your paycheck in advance toward taxes.

choices.text: Tax money taken out before you receive your paycheck
The interest rate on your savings account
A late fee on a bill

questions.title: Question 4
questions.prompt: Which item can reduce taxable income before certain taxes are calculated?
questions.explanation: Eligible pre-tax deductions can reduce taxable income.

lessonBlocks.heading: W-4, pay stubs, and benefit deductions
paragraphs: Your [[W-4]] affects how much federal income tax is withheld. It does not lock in your final tax bill forever, but it does affect take-home pay during the year.
Your [[Pay Stub]] is where you can verify taxes, health insurance deductions, retirement contributions, and whether your [[Direct Deposit]] amount matches expectations.
bullets: Two people with the same salary can have different net pay
Benefit elections affect take-home pay
Review your pay stub early to catch errors quickly

questions.title: Question 5
questions.prompt: Why might two workers with the same salary receive different net pay?
questions.explanation: Different withholding settings and deductions can change take-home pay.

choices.text: Salary always determines identical net pay
Net pay is random each month
Only job title changes paycheck amounts
They may have different withholding and benefit deductions

questions.title: Question 6
questions.prompt: What is a pay stub used for?
questions.explanation: A pay stub shows gross pay, deductions, taxes, and net pay.

choices.text: It is your final tax return
It shows how your paycheck was calculated

lessonBlocks.heading: Bonuses, RSUs, and taxable compensation
paragraphs: As your career grows, compensation may include bonuses or [[RSU]] grants. These can be exciting, but they also come with tax implications and timing differences.
A useful habit is separating “stable monthly pay” from “extra compensation.” Do not build fixed obligations around income that is irregular or not fully vested yet.
bullets: Base pay is better for recurring bills
Variable compensation is not the same as guaranteed cash
Compensation structure matters, not just headline salary

questions.title: Question 7
questions.prompt: Which type of income is usually least appropriate to rely on for fixed monthly bills?
questions.explanation: Irregular income such as bonuses is less dependable for fixed monthly obligations.

choices.text: Stable net pay from regular payroll

questions.title: Question 8
questions.prompt: What does RSU stand for?
questions.explanation: RSU stands for Restricted Stock Unit.

takeaway: Build budgets using net pay, not headline salary.
Understand the difference between taxes, withholding, and FICA.
Review your pay stub early and often.
Treat bonuses and RSUs as less predictable than base pay.

modules.title: 2. Living Expenses
modules.shortDescription: Learn what it actually costs to live on your own.

lessonBlocks.heading: Fixed vs variable expenses
paragraphs: As you relocate to a new city and start setting up your place, one of the most useful budget skills is separating [[Fixed Expense]] items from [[Variable Expense]] items.
Rent is usually fixed for the lease term. Groceries, gas, restaurants, electricity, wifi, and water can all change month to month.
bullets: Fixed expenses are easier to forecast
Variable expenses require ongoing attention
Utilities are often more volatile than people expect

questions.title: Question 1
questions.prompt: Which of the following is most likely a variable expense?
questions.explanation: Groceries usually change month to month, while rent is typically fixed by lease.

questions.title: Question 2
questions.prompt: Which category is commonly overlooked in first apartment budgeting?
questions.explanation: Utilities and move-in costs are often missed when people compare rent alone.

lessonBlocks.heading: Renting vs buying and hidden housing costs
paragraphs: For many new grads, renting is more practical than buying. Buying often involves down payment, closing costs, property taxes, maintenance, and less flexibility to move for work.
When renting, remember that sticker rent is only part of the housing story. [[Security Deposit]], parking, furniture, renter insurance, and commute costs all matter.
bullets: Cheap rent is not always cheapest overall
Buying has many costs beyond the monthly mortgage
Transportation can change the true cost of a home

questions.title: Question 3
questions.context: You are choosing between two apartments after moving for your first job.
questions.prompt: Which comparison is strongest?
questions.explanation: A good housing decision compares the full monthly cost, not just advertised rent.

choices.text: Choose the lowest rent and ignore commute
Pick the nicest apartment because you deserve it
Compare rent, utilities, commute, and move-in costs together
Choose based only on square footage

questions.title: Question 4
questions.prompt: Which cost is more associated with buying than renting?
questions.explanation: Closing costs are a classic home-buying cost.

lessonBlocks.heading: Necessities, lifestyle inflation, and cash flow timing
paragraphs: New grads often underestimate how much convenience spending can creep up. Restaurants, delivery, rideshares, and “small” recurring purchases can compete with necessities if you do not watch them.
Cash flow timing also matters. Even if your monthly income covers your bills on paper, poor timing can still create overdrafts or late fees.
bullets: Needs should be funded before wants
Weekly spending checks often work better than month-end surprises
Cash flow timing matters, not just total monthly income

questions.title: Question 5
questions.prompt: What is the strongest first move if restaurant spending keeps exceeding plan?
questions.explanation: A weekly cap plus a simple meal plan creates sustainable control.

choices.text: Set a weekly cap and plan a few simple meals
Ignore it and hope next month is better
Put food on a credit card and review later

questions.title: Question 6
questions.prompt: Which statement is most accurate about cash flow?
questions.explanation: Cash flow timing matters because bills can be due before your next paycheck arrives.

choices.text: Due dates do not matter if your salary is decent
Variable expenses never affect cash flow
Bill timing can create problems even if monthly income is enough overall

lessonBlocks.heading: Utilities, subscriptions, and recurring leaks
paragraphs: Electricity, water, internet, and subscriptions are easy to underestimate because each one may feel small in isolation.
A strong early-career habit is reviewing recurring charges regularly. Small monthly leaks can crowd out savings and emergency fund progress.
bullets: Recurring charges deserve review
Utilities can fluctuate with season and usage
Tiny leaks can become big annual totals

questions.title: Question 7
questions.prompt: Why are subscriptions often financially dangerous for beginners?
questions.explanation: Their small monthly cost can make them easy to ignore while they add up over time.

choices.text: They can quietly add up because each one feels small
They are fixed by law and cannot be cancelled
They directly lower your credit score

questions.title: Question 8
questions.prompt: Which utility is most likely to vary with weather and usage?
questions.explanation: Electricity bills often change with air conditioning, heating, and seasonal usage.

choices.text: A known annual fee card fee

takeaway: Separate fixed and variable expenses clearly.
Compare total housing cost, not rent alone.
Watch cash flow timing, not just monthly totals.
Recurring charges and convenience spending deserve regular review.

modules.title: 3. Banking & Credit Cards
modules.shortDescription: Use checking, savings, debit, and credit intentionally.

lessonBlocks.heading: Checking, savings, debit, and APY
paragraphs: Your [[Checking Account]] is your operating account. It is where [[Direct Deposit]] lands and where your [[Debit Card]] usually pulls from.
A [[Savings Account]] is designed for storing money and typically pays more interest, often shown as [[APY]]. That makes it better for reserves than checking.
bullets: Checking is for transactions
Savings is better for reserves
Higher APY matters more for money you can leave in place

questions.title: Question 1
questions.prompt: Which account type usually earns more interest?
questions.explanation: Savings accounts generally pay more interest than checking accounts.

questions.title: Question 2
questions.prompt: What is a debit card linked to?
questions.explanation: A debit card is usually linked to your checking account.

lessonBlocks.heading: Overdrafts, due dates, and keeping a buffer
paragraphs: One common early-career mistake is running a checking account too close to zero. An [[Overdraft]] can happen when a transaction exceeds your available balance, potentially triggering fees.
Keeping a small checking buffer and knowing every bill [[Due Date]] can help prevent avoidable fees.
bullets: Small buffers prevent expensive mistakes
Bill timing matters
Overdraft fees can quickly compound a shortfall

questions.title: Question 3
questions.prompt: What is an overdraft?
questions.explanation: An overdraft happens when a transaction exceeds the available account balance.

choices.text: A transaction exceeds your available balance

questions.title: Question 4
questions.prompt: What is the best reason to keep a small checking buffer?
questions.explanation: A checking buffer helps reduce the chance of overdrafts or timing-based payment problems.

choices.text: It replaces the need for savings
It helps avoid overdrafts and timing problems

lessonBlocks.heading: How credit cards work: APR, statement balance, minimum payment
paragraphs: A [[Credit Card]] is useful when managed carefully, but expensive when not. If you do not pay the [[Statement Balance]] in full, interest may be charged based on the [[APR]].
The [[Minimum Payment]] keeps the account current, but paying only the minimum usually slows debt payoff dramatically.
bullets: Paying in full avoids most purchase interest
APR matters if you carry a balance
Minimum payment is not the same as healthy repayment

questions.title: Question 5
questions.prompt: What does APR mean on a credit card?
questions.explanation: APR is the annual percentage cost of borrowing.

choices.text: A score assigned by a credit bureau
The annual percentage cost of borrowing

questions.title: Question 6
questions.prompt: What is the statement balance?
questions.explanation: It is the amount owed at the end of the billing cycle.

choices.text: The amount owed at the end of the billing cycle
Your annual fee total for life
The amount your employer pays to the card issuer

lessonBlocks.heading: Utilization, fees, and choosing your first card
paragraphs: [[Credit Utilization]] is the percentage of your available credit that you are currently using. Many people try to stay below 30% because lower utilization is generally healthier than running close to your limit.
When comparing cards, think about [[Annual Fee]], rewards, and [[Foreign Transaction Fee]]. The best card is not always the fanciest one.
bullets: Low utilization is generally better than high utilization
High annual fees require real benefit usage to make sense
Travel fees matter if you expect international spending

questions.title: Question 7
questions.prompt: If your credit limit is $2,000 and your balance is $800, your utilization is:

questions.title: Question 8
questions.context: You expect to travel internationally for work or vacation.
questions.prompt: Which fee matters specifically for purchases in another country or currency?
questions.explanation: Foreign transaction fees apply to international or foreign-currency purchases on some cards.

takeaway: Use checking for operations and savings for reserves.
Keep a checking buffer to avoid timing-based fees.
Understand APR, statement balance, and minimum payment before using credit.
Choose cards based on actual use, not flashy benefits alone.

modules.title: 4. Insurance & Benefits
modules.shortDescription: Protect yourself from financial shocks and use benefits wisely.

lessonBlocks.heading: Medical insurance basics for first-job adults
paragraphs: Health insurance can feel overwhelming at first, but a few concepts do most of the work: [[Premium]], [[Deductible]], [[Copay]], [[Coinsurance]], and [[Out-of-Pocket Maximum]].
Cheap monthly premium does not always mean cheap healthcare overall. A plan with a high deductible may cost less now but more later if you need care.
bullets: Premium is what you pay to keep coverage
Deductible is not the same as copay
Out-of-pocket maximum caps covered yearly spending

questions.title: Question 1
questions.prompt: What does a deductible mean?
questions.explanation: It is the amount you pay before the insurer starts sharing covered costs.

choices.text: The amount you pay before insurance starts sharing costs
The total tax you owe for healthcare

questions.title: Question 2
questions.prompt: Which term means the most you pay for covered care in a plan year?
questions.explanation: The out-of-pocket maximum caps your covered yearly spending.

lessonBlocks.heading: In-network care, trade-offs, and plan selection
paragraphs: [[In-Network]] care usually costs less because your insurer has negotiated rates with those providers.
As a new grad, a balanced plan is often easier to understand than choosing only by the lowest premium. The right choice depends on expected care usage, cash flow, and risk tolerance.
bullets: In-network care is usually cheaper
Lowest premium is not always best overall
Coverage should match your financial reality

questions.title: Question 3
questions.prompt: What does in-network usually mean?
questions.explanation: In-network providers have negotiated prices with your insurer.

choices.text: The provider is open on weekends
The provider has negotiated rates with your insurer
The provider works for your employer

questions.title: Question 4
questions.context: You are choosing between three plans during benefits enrollment.
questions.prompt: Which approach is strongest?
questions.explanation: A strong choice compares premium, deductible, and likely usage together.

choices.text: Choose the lowest premium without reading anything else
Choose the most expensive plan automatically
Compare premium, deductible, and expected care usage
Skip coverage because you are young

lessonBlocks.heading: 401(k), employer match, and HSA
paragraphs: A [[401(k)]] is one of the first investing tools many employees encounter. If your employer offers an [[Employer Match]], contributing enough to receive that match can be extremely valuable.
An [[HSA]] is different: it is tied to eligible health plans and can be used for qualified medical expenses.
bullets: Employer match is part of compensation
401(k) is for retirement
HSA is for eligible medical expenses under qualifying plans

questions.title: Question 5
questions.prompt: Which benefit is specifically for retirement saving?
questions.explanation: A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored retirement account.

questions.title: Question 6
questions.prompt: What is employer match?
questions.explanation: Employer match is money your employer adds to your retirement account based on your contribution.

choices.text: Money your employer adds to your retirement account based on your contribution
A tax refund for commuting to work
A bonus paid into your checking account every month

lessonBlocks.heading: Renter insurance and auto insurance
paragraphs: When you live on your own, insurance is not just about health. [[Renter Insurance]] helps protect your belongings and personal liability, while [[Auto Insurance]] helps cover driving-related risks.
These products are about transferring the cost of a severe loss you probably could not easily absorb on your own.
bullets: Renter insurance protects more than just furniture
Auto insurance includes liability concepts as well as vehicle damage coverage
Small premiums can protect against very large losses

questions.title: Question 7
questions.context: You just moved into your first apartment and bought a laptop and furniture.
questions.prompt: Which product most directly helps protect your belongings while renting?
questions.explanation: Renter insurance commonly helps cover personal property losses and liability.

questions.title: Question 8
questions.prompt: Why do people buy insurance in general?
questions.explanation: Insurance helps protect against losses that would be financially difficult to absorb alone.

choices.text: To reduce the impact of large financial losses

takeaway: Insurance choices should balance monthly cost and potential risk.
Understand premium, deductible, copay, and out-of-pocket maximum.
Employer match can be one of the highest-value benefits available.
Renter and auto insurance protect against losses most beginners cannot easily absorb.

modules.title: 5. Emergency Fund
modules.shortDescription: Build resilience before life tests your budget.

lessonBlocks.heading: What an emergency fund is for
paragraphs: As an early-career worker living independently, surprises hit harder because you may have fewer financial buffers. A broken laptop, urgent flight home, medical cost, or job interruption can quickly become debt without an [[Emergency Fund]].
Emergency savings are for urgent, necessary costs — not for convenience spending or planned fun.
bullets: Emergency = urgent and necessary
Emergency savings help reduce dependence on credit
The point is resilience, not perfection

questions.title: Question 1
questions.prompt: Which is the best example of an emergency fund use?
questions.explanation: Unexpected essential repairs are exactly what emergency savings are for.

questions.title: Question 2
questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of an emergency fund?
questions.explanation: Its purpose is to cover urgent, unexpected expenses without automatically creating debt.

lessonBlocks.heading: How much to save and what counts as essential expenses
paragraphs: A common rule of thumb is 3–6 months of essential expenses, not total lifestyle spending. Essentials often mean rent, food, utilities, transportation, insurance, and minimum debt payments.
If that target feels large, start with a smaller milestone. Even one month or a starter cushion can reduce risk meaningfully.
bullets: Essential expenses are different from total discretionary spending
A starter fund is better than waiting for the perfect number
Targets can scale as income rises

questions.title: Question 3
questions.prompt: A common guideline for emergency savings is:
questions.explanation: Many guidelines suggest 3–6 months of essential expenses.

choices.text: Whatever your annual bonus happens to be

questions.title: Question 4
questions.prompt: Which category is most likely part of essential expenses?
questions.explanation: Rent is a classic essential expense.

lessonBlocks.heading: Where to keep the money: liquidity over excitement
paragraphs: Emergency cash usually belongs somewhere stable and accessible, such as a savings account. [[Liquidity]] matters more here than chasing the highest possible return.
The role of emergency money is not to outperform the market. The role is to be available when real life happens.
bullets: Accessibility matters
Volatility can be dangerous for money you may need suddenly
Savings account use is about stability, not excitement

questions.title: Question 5
questions.prompt: Why is liquidity important for emergency funds?
questions.explanation: Emergency money should be easy to access quickly without major loss of value.

choices.text: It lets you access the money quickly when needed

questions.title: Question 6
questions.prompt: Which place is generally better for emergency cash than a volatile stock position?
questions.explanation: A savings account is usually more stable and accessible than volatile investments.

lessonBlocks.heading: Emergency savings vs insurance
paragraphs: Emergency funds and insurance work together. Savings help with immediate cash needs, while insurance reduces the scale of certain losses.
A resilient plan usually uses both: some liquid savings plus appropriate insurance coverage.
bullets: Savings handle cash flow shocks
Insurance handles certain high-cost risks
Neither one fully replaces the other

questions.title: Question 7
questions.prompt: Which statement is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Emergency savings and insurance solve different parts of the risk problem.

choices.text: Insurance removes the need for any emergency fund
An emergency fund removes the need for insurance
Savings and insurance play different protective roles
Neither one matters if your salary is decent

questions.title: Question 8
questions.prompt: Which is the strongest beginner strategy?
questions.explanation: A starter emergency fund plus core insurance creates a stronger base than relying on one tool alone.

choices.text: Build starter emergency savings while keeping core insurance coverage
Skip savings and rely only on credit cards
Skip insurance and hope emergencies do not happen
Invest all cash and assume you can sell anytime

takeaway: Emergency funds are for urgent, necessary expenses.
A 3–6 month guideline is common, but even a starter fund helps.
Keep emergency cash liquid and stable.
Savings and insurance work best together.

modules.title: 6. Fraud & Scams
modules.shortDescription: Protect your identity, accounts, and credit profile.

lessonBlocks.heading: Phishing and urgency traps
paragraphs: Scams often work because they feel urgent. A fake payroll issue, fake bank alert, or fake package notice can pressure you into clicking before thinking. That is the core of [[Phishing]].
A strong habit is to distrust the message itself and instead go directly to the known official app, portal, or phone number.
bullets: Urgency is a common scam tactic
Official-looking design does not prove authenticity
Go to trusted channels directly

questions.title: Question 1
questions.context: You receive an email saying your payroll details must be updated immediately through a link in the message.
questions.prompt: What is the safest first response?
questions.explanation: The safest move is to use the official payroll portal directly, not the link in the suspicious email.

choices.text: Click quickly to avoid payroll delays
Reply with bank details for faster processing
Forward it to friends for opinions
Go directly to the official HR/payroll portal

questions.title: Question 2
questions.prompt: Which is a classic phishing red flag?
questions.explanation: Urgency and pressure are common phishing tactics.

choices.text: A bill due date listed in your own budgeting app
An urgent warning pushing immediate action through a link
A scheduled employer benefits reminder in your HR portal
A known bank statement available in your official app

lessonBlocks.heading: Identity theft and the role of credit freezes
paragraphs: [[Identity Theft]] can lead to fake new accounts, credit damage, and a lot of cleanup work. A [[Credit Freeze]] can help reduce the chance that someone opens new credit in your name.
The three major credit bureaus are [[Equifax]], [[Experian]], and [[TransUnion]]. Knowing these names matters when responding to fraud.
bullets: Credit freezes help block fraudulent new credit applications
A freeze does not erase existing debt
You generally manage freezes bureau by bureau

questions.title: Question 3
questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a credit freeze?
questions.explanation: A credit freeze restricts access to your credit report to help prevent fraudulent new accounts.

choices.text: Restrict access to your credit report

questions.title: Question 4
questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three major U.S. credit bureaus?
questions.explanation: FICO is a scoring model company, not one of the three major credit bureaus.

lessonBlocks.heading: Practical protection habits
paragraphs: Fraud prevention is not only about recognizing scams. It is also about keeping your systems clean: unique passwords, device updates, bank alerts, and fast reporting if something looks wrong.
The earlier you react to suspicious activity, the easier it usually is to contain the damage.
bullets: Fast reporting matters
Account monitoring is part of financial literacy
Prevention habits reduce stress later

questions.title: Question 5
questions.prompt: Why is quick reporting of suspicious account activity important?
questions.explanation: Fast reporting can help reduce losses and limit damage.

choices.text: It always raises your credit score
It automatically recovers every dollar immediately
It can help contain damage sooner
It is only relevant for wealthy people

questions.title: Question 6
questions.prompt: Which habit most directly supports account security?
questions.explanation: Using strong unique passwords is a foundational security habit.

choices.text: Using the same password everywhere for convenience
Ignoring bank alerts until the weekend
Sharing login credentials with friends you trust

lessonBlocks.heading: Credit bureau literacy for recovery
paragraphs: If identity theft affects credit applications, bureau knowledge becomes practical, not theoretical. [[Experian]], [[Equifax]], and [[TransUnion]] are the places many fraud-response steps involve.
That is why fraud literacy is part of financial literacy: protecting access to future housing, loans, and even some job-related checks.
bullets: Credit bureau knowledge supports fraud response
Fraud can affect future borrowing and housing
Protection is part of long-term financial stability

questions.title: Question 7
questions.prompt: Why does credit fraud matter beyond just one stolen card?
questions.explanation: Identity-related fraud can affect future credit access and financial opportunities.

choices.text: Because it only changes your bank app theme
Because it can damage future credit access and financial options
Because it automatically cancels your job contract

questions.title: Question 8
questions.prompt: Which trio lists the major U.S. credit bureaus correctly?
questions.explanation: Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion are the three major U.S. credit bureaus.

takeaway: Urgency is one of the biggest scam red flags.
Use official channels directly instead of trusting suspicious links.
Credit freezes can help prevent fraudulent new accounts.
Fraud literacy protects future borrowing, housing, and financial stability.

modules.title: 7. Investing Basics
modules.shortDescription: Know the common tools early-career workers encounter.

lessonBlocks.heading: Starting with workplace investing
paragraphs: For many new grads, investing begins at work. A [[401(k)]] can help build retirement savings, and an [[Employer Match]] can add extra money if you contribute enough to receive it.
This is different from ordinary saving. Savings is about stability and access; investing is about long-term growth with risk.
bullets: 401(k) is for retirement, not emergency cash
Employer match increases benefit value
Long-term tools should match long-term goals

questions.title: Question 1
questions.prompt: Which account is specifically designed for retirement saving through an employer?
questions.explanation: A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored retirement account.

questions.title: Question 2
questions.prompt: What is employer match?
questions.explanation: It is money your employer contributes to your retirement account based on your contribution.

choices.text: Money your employer contributes based on your retirement contribution

lessonBlocks.heading: HSA, CDs, and what account type means
paragraphs: An [[HSA]] can be useful for eligible medical expenses, but it is tied to qualifying health plans. It is not the same as a normal savings account.
A [[Certificate of Deposit]] is a bank product with a fixed term and usually a fixed interest rate. It is different from stocks or mutual funds.
bullets: Account type matters as much as investment choice
CDs are deposit products, not stocks
HSA rules depend on health plan eligibility

questions.title: Question 3
questions.prompt: What does HSA stand for?
questions.explanation: HSA stands for Health Savings Account.

questions.title: Question 4
questions.prompt: A Certificate of Deposit is best described as:
questions.explanation: A CD is a bank deposit product with a fixed term and usually a fixed interest rate.

choices.text: A bank deposit product with a fixed term and interest rate

lessonBlocks.heading: Stocks, RSUs, funds, and diversification
paragraphs: Some compensation packages include [[RSU]] grants. That can be valuable, but it also concentrates more of your finances in one company if you already work there.
A [[Fund]] can spread money across many investments. That is where [[Diversification]] becomes useful: it reduces dependence on a single company or sector.
bullets: Employer stock can create concentration risk
Funds often provide broader exposure than single stocks
Diversification is a risk-management concept

questions.title: Question 5
questions.prompt: What does RSU stand for?
questions.explanation: RSU stands for Restricted Stock Unit.

questions.title: Question 6
questions.prompt: Which choice is usually the most diversified?
questions.explanation: A broad fund usually holds many investments, unlike a single stock.

lessonBlocks.heading: Matching tools to goals
paragraphs: A useful mental model is to match the tool to the goal. Emergency cash needs liquidity. Near-term goals may need stability. Long-term goals can usually tolerate more risk.
That is why new grads benefit from understanding the difference between short-term cash tools and long-term growth tools.
bullets: Match the product to the job
Do not treat emergency cash like long-term investment money
Time horizon changes what makes sense

questions.title: Question 7
questions.prompt: Which tool is usually more appropriate for emergency cash than long-term stock exposure?
questions.explanation: Emergency cash is usually better kept in stable, accessible accounts rather than volatile investments.

choices.text: A savings account or similar stable cash vehicle

questions.title: Question 8
questions.prompt: Why is diversification useful?
questions.explanation: Diversification helps reduce dependence on one investment or one company.

choices.text: It replaces the need for an emergency fund

takeaway: Workplace investing often begins with a 401(k) and employer match.
Account type matters: HSA, CD, and investment funds serve different purposes.
RSUs can be valuable but may increase concentration risk.
Diversification helps reduce reliance on one company or asset.
